\chapter{Five Numbers, No New Signs}
\label{ch:ja-numbers-one-to-five}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say and write one to five in Japanese, and I can say which number has a native word standing beside its borrowed reading.}

Run ichi to go in order, then name the two of the five that were already yours and say where you had met each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ichi]{\ja{いち} — one, taken out of a word you already say}

\label{lesson:JA-C14-ichi}



\begin{quote}
Two recalls, at two distances.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the nine family words — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} the whole doorway exchange, start to finish — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{いち}} — \emph{ichi} — \textbf{one}
\end{quote}

Say \textbf{\ja{もういちど}}. You have asked for one more time since chapter nine, and that lesson told you what the first two morae were: \emph{ichi} is \textbf{one}. Nothing about the word changes today. It stops being part of a phrase and starts being a number you can use on its own.

Both signs are yours: \textbf{\ja{い} + \ja{ち}}.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Read \textbf{\ja{い} | \ja{ち}}. Copy \textbf{\ja{いち}}, hide it, and write it from the meaning. Then say \textbf{\ja{いちど}} and point to the part of it that is the number.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did this lesson need? (\textbf{None.})

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%84\%E3\%81\%A1}{Wiktionary: \ja{いち}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[go]{\ja{ご} — five, and the sign that was holding it}

\label{lesson:JA-C14-go}



\begin{quote}
Two recalls, then the second number.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{one} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the farewell, and say it after hearing it — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{ご}} — \emph{go} — \textbf{five}
\end{quote}

Write \textbf{\ja{五}} once. Chapter five taught you those four strokes, gave you the sound \emph{go}, said on the page that \textbf{the sign means five on its own}, and then asked you for nothing but the sound, because it was only there to cue the \emph{go} inside \textbf{\ja{語}}.

That was the whole of the deferral. \textbf{\ja{五}} is \textbf{five}, and you have been able to write it for nine chapters.

In hiragana it is \textbf{\ja{こ}} with the dakuten: \textbf{\ja{ご}}. Both marks are yours.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{五}} from memory: top, turn, middle, long bottom. Then write \textbf{\ja{ご}} and say \emph{go}. Say \textbf{\ja{いち}}, then \textbf{\ja{ご}} — the two numbers you owned before this chapter opened.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did this lesson need? (\textbf{None.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%94}{Wiktionary: \ja{ご}}; \href{https://kanjivg.tagaini.net/kanjivg/kanji/04e94.html}{KanjiVG stroke-order data}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ni]{\ja{に} — two, one mora long}

\label{lesson:JA-C14-ni}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls, then the third number.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{five} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the fourteen body words — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{よ}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{に}} — \emph{ni} — \textbf{two}
\end{quote}

One mora, one sign, and you learned that sign in chapter two to build \textbf{\ja{こんにちは}}. Say the three numbers you now have, in the order you met them: \emph{ichi}, \emph{go}, \emph{ni}.

Do not let the shortness fool you into hurrying it. \textbf{\ja{に}} is one full beat, exactly as long as either beat of \textbf{\ja{いち}}.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Read \textbf{\ja{に}}. Write it, hide it, write it again from the meaning. Then say \emph{ichi — ni} and hold both at one beat each.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs has this chapter needed? (\textbf{None.})

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%AB}{Wiktionary: \ja{に}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[san]{\ja{さん} — three, on two old signs}

\label{lesson:JA-C14-san}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the fourth number.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{two} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} take the family reception once more — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write full-size \textbf{\ja{つ}} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{な}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{さん}} — \emph{san} — \textbf{three}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ja{さ}} came in chapter four for \textbf{\ja{ありがとうございます}}; \textbf{\ja{ん}} came in chapter two, and its lesson said it is the one hiragana sign that is not a full syllable. It still is not. \textbf{\ja{さん}} is \textbf{two beats}: \emph{sa}, then a beat of the nasal on its own.

Say \emph{ichi — ni — san}. Four numbers, four lessons, no new signs.

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Read \textbf{\ja{さ} | \ja{ん}} as two beats. Write \textbf{\ja{さん}}, hide it, write it again. Then say \emph{ichi, ni, san} three times without slowing at \textbf{\ja{ん}}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which four numbers do you now have? (\emph{\textbf{Ichi, ni, san, go}}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%81\%95\%E3\%82\%93}{Wiktionary: \ja{さん}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yon]{\ja{よん} — four, and where the two systems meet}

\label{lesson:JA-C14-yon}



\begin{quote}
Four recalls, then the number with two names.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{three} — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} run the nine family words — \textbf{R2}, five lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my father} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} write \textbf{\ja{ら}} — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll Want to Know — hear and say}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{よん}} — \emph{yon} — \textbf{four}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ja{し}} — \emph{shi} — \textbf{four}, the same number said the other way
\end{quote}

Both signs of \textbf{\ja{よん}} are yours, and so is \textbf{\ja{し}}. Two beats each: \emph{yo} plus the nasal beat, or \emph{shi} alone.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — a native word inside a borrowed count}]
Japanese has two ways of reading a sign: the reading it borrowed from Chinese along with the sign, and the reading it already had for the thing the sign means. Wiktionary's readings box for the kanji \textbf{four} lists them side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{reading} & \textbf{kind} & \textbf{which} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ja{し}} \emph{shi} & on'yomi, borrowed with the sign & four \\
\textbf{\ja{よん}} \emph{yon} & kun'yomi, the native word & four \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Ichi}, \emph{ni}, \emph{san} and \emph{go} are all borrowed readings, and none of them has a native word standing beside it in the everyday count. \textbf{Four is the first place in the run where the native word is used too} — and in ordinary speech \textbf{\ja{よん}} is the one you will hear far more often.

That split is coming back. It is the same seam the counters run along, and it opens here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn — read, copy, recall}
Write \textbf{\ja{よん}} and \textbf{\ja{し}}. Say the run in order: \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go}. Then say it once with \textbf{\ja{し}} in place of \textbf{\ja{よん}} and hear how much closer \emph{shi} sits to \emph{ichi}.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which four is a native Japanese word? (\textbf{\ja{よん}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E5\%9B\%9B}{Wiktionary: the kanji read shi and yon}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E3\%82\%88\%E3\%82\%93}{Wiktionary: \ja{よん}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{One to five, in order at last}

\label{lesson:JA-R14-one-to-five}



\begin{quote}
Three recalls before the run.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{four}, both ways — \textbf{R1}, one lesson back
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{my father} — \textbf{R3}, twenty lessons back
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ja{さようなら}} off the page — \textbf{R4}, eighty lessons back
\end{itemize}

Nothing new arrives here. This is the first time the five stand in numerical order, and that has been deliberate.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn — the run, and the two you started with}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ichi ni san yon go} — the run, without stopping
  \item \emph{Say it:} it again with \textbf{\ja{し}} at four
  \item \emph{Write it:} \textbf{\ja{五}}, and say which of the five it is
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter, in one number}]
\textbf{Five numbers, and zero new signs.} Every mark in \emph{ichi, ni, san, yon, go} was taught before this chapter opened, and two of the five words were already in your hands: \emph{ichi} inside \textbf{\ja{もういちど}}, and \emph{go} as the kanji \textbf{\ja{五}}.

One thing did arrive that is not a word: at \textbf{four}, the native reading stands beside the borrowed one. Watch for it again.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many new signs did this chapter cost? (\textbf{None}.) Which number in the run has a native word beside its borrowed reading? (\textbf{Four}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
